title: Error Handling
summary: Catch runtime errors with try/catch, throw your own errors with clear messages, and clean up with finally.
intro: Real input is messy: broken JSON, missing fields, numbers out of range. Instead of letting one bad line crash the whole program, you catch the error, report it, and keep going.

steps.title: try and catch

example.title: Reading user names
example.prompt: Read one JSON object per line and print the user's name, or the name of the error when the line cannot be read, then print done.
example.output:
name: Ada
error: TypeError
error: SyntaxError
name: Linus
done
example.explanation: Each line gets its own `try`, so one bad line cannot stop the loop. `{"user":null}` parses fine, but `data.user.name` reads a property of `null` and throws a TypeError. The third line is cut off, so `JSON.parse` throws a SyntaxError before anything prints. After each catch the loop moves on, and `done` prints at the end.

practice.title: First items
practice.prompt:
Read one JSON snippet per line and print its first item, or the name of the error, then count the good and bad lines.

1. For each line, parse it with `JSON.parse` and print `first: <value>` using `data.items[0]`.
2. If anything throws, print `error: <error name>` instead.
3. Count the lines that printed a value as good and the ones that failed as bad.
4. After the loop print `good: <good>, bad: <bad>`.

Input:

```text
{"items":[3,5]}
{"items":null}
[1,2
```

Expected output:

```text
first: 3
error: TypeError
error: SyntaxError
good: 1, bad: 2
```

tests.output:
first: 3
error: TypeError
error: SyntaxError
good: 1, bad: 2

first: 7
first: 10
error: TypeError
good: 2, bad: 1

error: TypeError
error: SyntaxError
good: 0, bad: 2

hints: Put both the `JSON.parse` call and the `console.log` inside one `try` block.
Increase `good` right after printing inside `try`, and increase `bad` inside `catch`.
Reading `items[0]` from `null` or from a missing `items` throws a TypeError.

steps.title: Throwing your own errors

example.title: Bank withdrawals
example.prompt: Read a starting balance, then one withdrawal per line, and print the new balance or the error each withdrawal raised.
example.output:
balance: 70
TypeError: amount must be a number
RangeError: insufficient funds
RangeError: amount must be positive
balance: 50
example.explanation: `withdraw` checks its arguments first and throws before changing anything. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, so the first check throws a TypeError. 500 is more than 70, so the last check throws a RangeError. Without the check for `amount <= 0`, a withdrawal of -5 would quietly add money. A failed withdrawal skips the assignment, so the balance stays at 70 until the last line takes 20.

practice.title: Checking ages
practice.prompt:
Read one age per line and print it, or the error that explains why it is not valid.

1. Write `parseAge(text)` that converts `text` with `Number`.
2. If the result is `NaN`, throw a `TypeError` with the message `age must be a number`.
3. If the age is below 0 or above 150, throw a `RangeError` with the message `age must be 0 to 150`.
4. Otherwise return the age.
5. For each line print `age: <age>`, or `<error name>: <error message>` when `parseAge` throws.

Input:

```text
36
abc
200
```

Expected output:

```text
age: 36
TypeError: age must be a number
RangeError: age must be 0 to 150
```

tests.output:
age: 36
TypeError: age must be a number
RangeError: age must be 0 to 150

age: 0
age: 150
RangeError: age must be 0 to 150

TypeError: age must be a number
age: 7

hints: Use `Number.isNaN(age)` for the type check, since `NaN` is still a number to `typeof`.
Write `throw new RangeError("age must be 0 to 150")` for the range check. 0 and 150 are allowed.
In the loop, call `parseAge(line)` inside `try` and print `${error.name}: ${error.message}` in `catch`.

steps.title: finally, rethrowing, and causes

example.title: Order intake
example.prompt: Read orders as item and quantity lines, reject bad quantities, close every order, and stop with a fatal message when an order cannot be read at all.
example.output:
order 1: 2 x pen
closed order 1
rejected: bad quantity 0
closed order 2
closed order 3
fatal: cannot read order 3 (cause: TypeError)
example.explanation: The inner catch only handles RangeError, so `cup 0` is rejected and the loop goes on. `book` has no quantity, which throws a TypeError. The inner catch wraps it in a new Error with the original as its `cause`. `finally` still prints `closed order 3` before the wrapped error reaches the outer catch, which reads `error.cause.name`. The loop is over at that point, so `lamp 1` and `all orders read` never run.

practice.title: Loading configs
practice.prompt:
Read one JSON config per line, skip broken JSON, and stop with a fatal message on any other error.

1. Write `loadConfig(text)` that parses `text` with `JSON.parse` and throws a `RangeError` when `port` is not a whole number from 1 to 65535. Otherwise return the config.
2. In an outer `try`, loop over `lines.entries()` and call `loadConfig` in an inner `try` that prints `port: <port>`.
3. In the inner `catch`, print `bad json` for a `SyntaxError`. Wrap any other error with `new Error("cannot load config <n>", { cause: error })`, where n counts lines from 1.
4. Give the inner `try` a `finally` that prints `done`.
5. After the loop print `all configs loaded`. In the outer `catch` print `fatal: <message> (cause: <cause name>)`.

Input:

```text
{"port":8080}
{"port":
{"port":70000}
{"port":443}
```

Expected output:

```text
port: 8080
done
bad json
done
done
fatal: cannot load config 3 (cause: RangeError)
```

tests.output:
port: 8080
done
bad json
done
done
fatal: cannot load config 3 (cause: RangeError)

port: 80
done
port: 3000
done
all configs loaded

bad json
done
done
fatal: cannot load config 2 (cause: TypeError)

hints: Copy the shape of the order example: the outer `try` wraps the whole loop.
Check `error instanceof SyntaxError` in the inner catch and throw the wrapped error in the else branch.
A line of `null` parses fine, but reading `port` from it throws a TypeError, which becomes the cause.

recap:
- An uncaught error stops the program, prints a stack trace to stderr, and exits with a failure code.
- `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` handles it, and the program continues after the catch.
- Print `error.name` for built-in errors: SyntaxError, TypeError, RangeError, ReferenceError.
- `throw new TypeError(message)` or `new RangeError(message)` after checking arguments at the top of a function.
- `finally` always runs, and it runs before an outer catch receives an escaping error.
- Check `error instanceof RangeError`, handle what you can, and rethrow the rest.
- `new Error(message, { cause: error })` adds context, and `error.cause` reads it back.
- `catch { ... }` without a binding when the error object does not matter.
